tip: 'Nació mi sobrina' puts the verb first – Spanish often places the subject after the verb when it's the new information. English keeps subject-first order.
Combing someone else's hair? 'Le' claims ownership: 'le peiné el pelo' – the 'le' says it's my daughter's, so no 'su pelo' needed.
No passive needed: 'me multaron' = they fined me. Spanish uses an anonymous 'they' where English reaches for 'I got fined.'
'Me quedé en blanco' – I stayed in blank. 'Quedarse' marks the state you end up in; here, going blank mid-presentation.
Passive participles agree like adjectives: 'la reunión fue cancelada' – 'cancelada', feminine, matching 'la reunión'. 'Cancelado' would grate.
With reflexive verbs and body parts, Spanish uses the definite article ('la cara'), not a possessive ('mi cara'). The reflexive 'me' already tells you whose face.
'Echó una mano' – threw a hand? 'Echar' is Spanish's do-everything verb; 'echar una mano' = lend a hand. You throw it, you don't lend it.
Spanish has a single verb for getting up early: 'madrugar'. 'Hay que madrugar' = you have to get up early – one word, no phrase needed.
'La aduana nos hizo abrir' – 'hacer' + infinitive = make someone do something. The person forced to act appears as a pronoun ('nos') before 'hacer'.
English 'became' is one verb; Spanish picks by type. 'Se puso contento' – 'ponerse' is for quick, temporary mood shifts, not lasting change.
Imperfect for background descriptions: 'hacía calor', 'estaban abiertas'.
'Saber' in the preterite isn't 'knew' – it's found out. 'Supe la verdad' = the moment the truth hit me. Ongoing knowledge would be 'sabía'.
'Tal... que' (such... that) sets up a cause and the result it leads to.
Things in general take the article: 'los celulares' = cellphones as a category. English drops 'the' for generalizations; Spanish usually keeps it.
'Me tocó organizar' – literally 'it touched me to organize.' 'Tocar' means the task fell to you by luck or duty, not by choice.
'Llover sobre mojado' = when bad things pile up on existing problems.
This 'fue' isn't 'ser' – it's 'ir': the interview WENT very well. 'Ser' and 'ir' share the same preterite ('fui', 'fue'), so only context tells you was vs went.
Wine is ordered by the 'copa' – the stemmed glass – and just 'una copa' on its own implies alcohol. A 'vaso' is a plain tumbler; 'vaso de vino' sounds rustic.
'La carta' is the menu in a restaurant. 'El menú' often refers to a fixed-price meal ('menú del día').
'De pequeño' = literally 'of small' = when I was little. 'De' + adjective is Spanish's shortcut for 'as a child' – no when-I-was clause needed.
Hunger is something you HAVE, not something you ARE: 'tenía hambre' = I had hunger. Same with thirst, fear, sleep – 'tener', never 'estar'.
'Carro' = car in Latin America; in Spain a 'carro' is a horse-drawn cart and cars are 'coches'. Say 'carro' in Mexico, 'coche' in Madrid.
'Por aquí' = around here / this way. 'Por' for approximate location or direction.
English needs 'had been living'; Spanish keeps plain imperfect + 'desde hacía': 'vivía sola desde hacía años' = she lived alone since it-made years.
'Ya' + imperfect ('sabía') for prior state + preterite ('llamaste') for the moment of calling.
Literally 'the saint went off to heaven on me' – the standard idiom for your mind going blank mid-thought. That's why it leads straight to forgetting 'la cita'.
Questions flip the order: verb first, subject after. 'Cierra la catedral' = closes the cathedral. There's no 'does' helper – the flip IS the question.
'Para' = for (employer): 'Trabajo para Google.' 'Para' for who you work for.
'Para' indicates purpose/destination. 'For three nights' = the intended duration of the stay.
No 'how to' needed: 'saber' + infinitive already means knowing HOW. 'No sabía usar la impresora' = I didn't know to-use the printer. Adding 'cómo' sounds English.
